html:
The written examinations that chose officials for the Chinese state, used from the Sui dynasty until they were abolished in 1905. In principle, any man who passed could rise to high office, whatever his birth.

The Han had already recruited officials by recommendation and testing, but the Sui first used written exams in earnest. Under the Tang they became a regular path to office. Under the Song they became the main one, organised as a ladder of local, provincial and palace exams, with names on papers hidden to stop favouritism.

Candidates were tested on the Confucian classics, and from the 14th century on the commentaries of Zhu Xi. Success took years of memorising and writing practice, so in practice it favoured families who could pay for study.

Its effects:

  • It weakened the old hereditary aristocracy and the military, and raised a class of scholar-officials.
  • It gave officials across a huge empire a shared culture of texts and style.
  • It made learning the road to status, which shaped family life, schooling and printing for centuries.

Korea, under Goryeo and Joseon, and Vietnam copied the system. European writers on China admired it, and it helped inspire merit-based civil service exams in Britain in the 19th century. The Qing ended it in 1905 as part of late reforms, a step that helped cut the old elite loose from the dynasty just before the 1911 revolution.
sum: The written examinations that chose officials for the Chinese state, used from the Sui dynasty until they were abolished in 1905. In principle, any man who passed could rise to high office, whatever his birth.
